answer.rationale:
The binding constraints are 14 days to expiry and a line at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer. That combination makes any action requiring qualification, onboarding, or dual-allocation setup (switch_primary_vendor, add_second_source) a delivery-risk increase this cycle regardless of its unit-cost appeal, and defer_decision is not available because this contract does not auto-renew (memory_c5's month-to-month fallback applied to a non-critical service, not the primary line). That leaves renew_incumbent or negotiate_terms, and negotiate_terms strictly dominates: it is the same continuity as renewal (memory_c1) plus the price and payment-term movement that benchmarking previously produced (memory_c4), with multi-year volume tiers (memory_c6) available as a lever toward the 18% target.

I verify memory_c2 and memory_c4 because they are the two most load-bearing and the two most likely to be misleading. memory_c2 is the strongest apparent answer to an 18% mandate and would justify switching, so I need the original record: whether that sharp unit-cost cut was measured on comparable volume and spec, whether 'onboarding was quick' meant weeks or a single cycle, and whether it covered this constrained component at committed volume. A summary that flattens a small-volume, low-criticality win into a general rule would be exactly the trap here. memory_c4 is the record I am about to act on, so I want the actual magnitude recovered and what benchmarking inputs were needed \% enough for a 14-day negotiation, or a multi-month exercise \% before I claim it can carry an 18% cut.

Downstream value risk: an 18% spend cut extracted under a hard deadline is the classic setup for quiet scope erosion \% expedite fees, buffer stock, engineering support, or quality-inspection coverage traded away in terms that read as price wins. memory_c6 asserts a longer term cut unit cost 'without narrowing the service scope,' but that is precisely the claim a consolidated summary is most likely to have smoothed over, so I will not lock a multi-year term unless scope is enumerated line by line against the current agreement. I also treat the incumbent's single-source position as an unresolved exposure: memory_c3's shortage lesson remains valid even though acting on it now would be reckless.

Uncertainty I am carrying forward rather than resolving: whether the low-cost vendor is genuinely cheaper at this spec and volume, and whether 18% is achievable from the incumbent at all. If negotiation lands short of target, the correct next-cycle move is a qualification trial of the alternate vendor sized to spare capacity \% built now as a fallback, not executed this cycle. I will record the negotiated terms with the scope baseline attached so the next session inherits evidence rather than a verdict.
